title: The bound no dispatch order can beat: how much of the environment-capacity tail of an agent batch is work, at the shipped slot counts

glossary.batch makespan $T$: the wall-clock time from the first task's start to the last task's completion in a batch of agent tasks
glossary.environment capacity $C_E$: the number of tool or sandbox jobs the harness runs at once (MCP-Atlas live: 3; the official runner's default: 5)
glossary.sample concurrency $C_S$: the number of admitted tasks holding a slot in the harness from admission to completion
glossary.capacity separation: the card paper's change: two caps ($C_S$ for admitted tasks, $C_E$ for running tool jobs) instead of one
glossary.chain: one task's trajectory: $n_k$ turns, each an inference segment of duration $\tau_{k,m}$ (holds no environment slot) followed by a tool segment of duration $g_{k,m}$ (holds one slot)
glossary.critical path $\\mathrm{CP}_k$: $\sum_{m=1}^{n_k} (\tau_{k,m} + g_{k,m})$, the time chain $k$ needs with no waiting at all
glossary.slot work $W$: $\sum_k \sum_m g_{k,m}$, the total slot-seconds the batch's tool jobs need
glossary.makespan lower bound $T_{\\mathrm{LB}}$: $\max\{W / C_E,\ \max_k \mathrm{CP}_k\}$: no dispatch order of tool jobs finishes before the slots have done all the work or before the longest chain has run (the parallel-machine bound of scheduling theory, $P \mid \mathrm{chains} \mid C_{\max}$)
glossary.FCFS: first-come-first-served dispatch of pending tool jobs
glossary.CAAS: the card paper's rule: pending tool jobs sorted by 30-second arrival band, then most completed turns, then shortest mean inference time, then FCFS (eq. 16)
glossary.hindsight list schedule: a dispatch order computed with every $\tau$, $g$ and $n_k$ known in advance: longest remaining critical path first (LRCP) or largest remaining slot work first (LPT)
glossary.ordering headroom $H$: $T_{\mathrm{FCFS}} / T_{\mathrm{LB}} - 1$, an upper bound on the share of makespan any order can remove
glossary.capture ratio $\\rho$: $(T_{\mathrm{FCFS}} - T_{\mathrm{rule}}) / (T_{\mathrm{FCFS}} - T_{\mathrm{hind}})$, the share of the achievable gain a rule takes
glossary.tail share $L_5 / T$: the share of makespan between 95% and 100% of tasks completing (derived from the card's Table 3: 40% and 27% after capacity separation, 8% before)
glossary.trace replay: a discrete-event simulation that re-runs recorded chains with their recorded $\tau$ and $g$ under a chosen dispatch rule and slot count

statement: On recorded agent batches with per-turn inference and tool durations, replay the chains under $C_E \in \{3, 5, 10, 25, 50\}$ slots with $C_S$ unbounded and compute, per cell, $T_{\mathrm{FCFS}}$, $T_{\mathrm{CAAS}}$ (eq. 16 reimplemented), the hindsight list schedules $T_{\mathrm{LRCP}}$ and $T_{\mathrm{LPT}}$, a random order, the bound $T_{\mathrm{LB}}$, the headroom $H$, the capture ratio $\rho_{\mathrm{CAAS}}$ and the tail share $L_5 / T$, with 20 bootstrap resamples of chains into batches of the trace's size. Add a shedding arm that drops the longest 5% of chains by $\mathrm{CP}_k$ and report its makespan saving beside $H$, so the two levers the lane argues about (reorder the tail, or shed it as the labs do under length censoring, pressure #10) are priced on one trace. Random given: recorded durations held fixed under every order and slot count (the card paper's own replay protocol, sec. 5.1), so $H$ is a property of the (trace, $C_E$) pair and the headline names both; the live check of that assumption (tool durations at $C_E = 3$ against $C_E = 5$) is step 2.
claim: At three tool slots on MCP-Atlas-shaped batches the makespan bound no dispatch order can beat sits within 10% of FCFS, so reordering tool jobs cannot remove more than a tenth of the makespan and the 27-40% tail share is the long chains' own work; the headroom opens only as $C_E$ grows toward the number of chains, where longest-chain-first hindsight rules take most of it.
trick: Add up all the tool-seconds, divide by the number of slots, compare with the longest single task, and see whether first-come-first-served was already within a tenth of that number before anyone reorders anything.
why_now: 2611.16661 (2026-11-12) ships CAAS, compares it with FCFS only, holds every recorded duration in a replay harness that could have computed the bound, and leaves a derived tail share of 27-40% unexplained; 2609.10964 (2026-09-10, HTML read 2026-11-16) ships a second tail-aware release rule for agentic workflows with no oracle or bound in its text; the GPU-side tail literature already reports oracle-normalized numbers (TIDE 2611.17924, 2026-11-13: 'up to 97% of optimal throughput') while the environment-side tail has none.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 ($0, 2 days): write to the 2611.16661 authors for the 495 MCP-Atlas replay records (stage sequences, recorded durations) — the re-open test and the lab arm; in parallel verify which public traces carry both inference and tool durations per turn: SWE-agent and mini-swe-agent trajectories (execution_time per step; the 2609.10964 traces report a mean tool gap of 1.3 s on SWE-bench, so this is the short-tool regime where $\max_k \mathrm{CP}_k$ binds), HAL archives (timestamps to verify), Terminal-Bench sessions with tool gaps (used in replay by 2611.02543; release to verify). Step 1 ($0, 0 GPU-h, 3 days): the discrete-event replay above on every trace obtained; the deliverable is the $H$-versus-$C_E / N$ curve with $\rho_{\mathrm{CAAS}}$, $\rho_{\mathrm{LRCP}}$ and the shedding arm on it. Step 2 (optional, about 30-50 GPU-h, judgment; MCP service keys and their rate limits are the unknown dollar line; 4 days): record own MCP-Atlas batches with an open 30B-class model under the official runner at $C_E = 3$ and $C_E = 5$ with per-turn timestamps, replay them as in step 1, and compare recorded tool durations across the two slot counts (the Gate 0 check that durations do not depend on concurrency).
killing_experiment.dollars: $0 for steps 0-1; step 2 about $150 of GPU time at spot rates plus MCP service usage (unknown)
killing_experiment.kills_if: Dead as written if $H \geq 0.25$ at $C_E = 3$ on MCP-Atlas-shaped traces (the authors' or own) with the bootstrap lower bound above 0.15: ordering is then a live lever at the shipped default and the headline flips to the pre-registered alternative (CAAS captures under 0.3 of the achievable gain), which is still the first oracle bound for the environment-side tail. Uninformative, and said so, if $T_{\mathrm{LRCP}} / T_{\mathrm{LB}} - 1 > 0.15$ at $C_E = 3$: the bracket between the bound and the best hindsight list schedule is then too wide to decide, and the next step is an exact or LP bound on the smaller trace. Dead at Gate 0 if step 2 shows recorded tool durations rising by more than 20% at the median from $C_E = 3$ to $C_E = 5$: replay then does not transfer to live batches at the shipped default.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment 0.5: $H < 0.10$ at $C_E = 3$ (with about 50 admitted chains and 7 in inference per the card's Table 3, three slots are busy whenever at least three chains have a ready tool job, so idle slot-time appears only when the remaining chains number under about $C_E (1 + \bar\tau / \bar g)$ — a few chains' alternation at the very end, small against a 163-minute batch), with $\rho_{\mathrm{CAAS}}$ undefined or near 1 because the achievable gain is itself a few percent; judgment 0.3: $0.10 \leq H < 0.25$; judgment 0.2: $H \geq 0.25$ with $\rho_{\mathrm{CAAS}} < 0.3$. In every case $H$ rises with $C_E / N$ and the shedding arm removes more makespan than any reordering at $C_E = 3$ (judgment 0.7).

title: The setting the validation never named: re-scoring Genie Sim Benchmark tasks under the physics time step, solver iterations and contact offset the platform ships but does not publish

glossary.Score: Genie Sim's task metric: the mean over episodes and scored stages of the stage credit $c_{is}$ (card, sec. II-C), in $[0, 1]$.
glossary.real-sim gap: $\Delta_i = \mathrm{Sim}_i - \mathrm{Real}_i$ for one (robot, task) pair; the paper reports MAE 0.0405 over 22 pairs, the README claims 'less than 10%'.
glossary.physics time step: the interval $h$ at which the engine integrates the rigid-body equations; the paper's object study uses 1 ms, the task layer's value is not stated.
glossary.solver iterations: the number of passes the contact solver makes per step (PhysX position/velocity iterations; the paper's object study: TGS 32/1).
glossary.contact offset: the distance at which PhysX begins generating contacts before surfaces touch; SimuGuard found a collision-detection constant of this kind decisive.
glossary.repeat floor: the Score difference between two runs of the same policy at the same setting with the same initial layouts; GPU PhysX is not bit-repeatable (GPUSimBench), so this is the smallest difference that means anything.
glossary.one-at-a-time: change one setting from the shipped value, hold the rest; the attribution method 2610.32277 Table 2 published.
glossary.shipped range: the values Isaac Lab and Isaac Sim ship as defaults and the paper's own values: $h \in \{1, 4, 8.3\}$ ms; position iterations $\in \{4, 16, 32\}$; contact offset at the asset default and at twice it.

statement: Install the released Genie Sim Benchmark (Isaac Sim 6.2), read the shipped physics setting $\theta_0 = (h, N_{\mathrm{pos}}, N_{\mathrm{vel}}, d_{\mathrm{contact}}, \mathrm{GPU/CPU})$ from the benchmark runtime and the per-robot physics payloads, pick 8 contact-rich released tasks (textile, stacking, handover, drawer first) and one policy per task fine-tuned the paper's way (pi0.5 SFT on real AgiBot World episodes where the task exists there, else on the released synthetic data, flagged as sim-trained), and evaluate each policy for $n = 100$ episodes with fixed initial layouts at $\theta_0$ twice (repeat floor) and at each one-at-a-time change of $h$, $N_{\mathrm{pos}}$, $d_{\mathrm{contact}}$ and GPU/CPU within the shipped range. Report per task and knob the paired Score shift $\delta_{t,k} = \mathrm{Score}_t(\theta_k) - \mathrm{Score}_t(\theta_0)$ with its bootstrap interval, against the repeat floor and against the two validity numbers the platform publishes (MAE 0.04; 'less than 10%'); report MAE and $r$ recomputed with the paper's real column where the task is one of the 22 pairs, noting that $r$ is invariant to any shift common to all tasks.
claim: On Genie Sim Benchmark the time step and contact offset move simulated task Scores of contact-rich tasks by more than the real-to-sim discrepancy the platform claims, while solver iterations move nothing above the repeat floor — so the published validity number certifies a setting the platform never names.
trick: Take the benchmark that says 'our simulator matches the real robot to within 10 points', change the physics knobs it never told you about within the range its own engine ships, and see whether the scores move by more than 10 points.
why_now: 2611.15020 (2026-11-11) is the first validity paper to name its numerics in one layer (1 ms, TGS 32/1, solref/solimp, a 20x cross-engine swing) and report task Scores from an unnamed engine and setting in the other; Genie Sim v3.5.0 (2026-11-02, README fetched) released the benchmark with task-selected runtimes (PhysX / Newton / MuJoCo) and RoboColiseum leaderboards score policies on it; 2610.32277 (2026-10-23) published the one-at-a-time harness method with the time step decisive for sim-trained trackers; SimuGuard (2026-10-30) shipped one-parameter rerun tooling; X2Real (2026-09) is the second correlation table of the autumn (0.84). Flag: the paper's own 22 policies are not released, so the probe reads the benchmark's sensitivity with a rebuilt policy, not the paper's exact table.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 ($0, 0 GPU-h, 2 days): bring up `geniesim docker` (Isaac Sim 6.2); list the released benchmark tasks and choose 8 contact-rich ones by a written rule (a grasp-and-transport or deformation stage in the task's stage list; textile first); read $\theta_0$ from the benchmark runtime config and `payloads/Physics/physx.usda`; record the engine per task (Isaac / Newton / MuJoCo runtimes); check whether RoboColiseum baseline weights cover the chosen tasks and whether the real AgiBot World dataset has matching tasks. Dead at step 0 if the benchmark runtime exposes no physics setting to the user. Step 1 (policies; 0-80 GPU-h, 0-5 days): if no baseline covers a task, fine-tune pi0.5 with OpenPI on the matching real AgiBot World episodes (the paper's recipe; about 10 GPU-h per task, judgment) or, where no real data exist, on the released synthetic episodes (flagged sim-trained, because a sim-trained policy can exploit $\theta_0$ and that is a different quantity). Step 2 (repeat floor; about 6 GPU-h, 1 day): 100 episodes per task at $\theta_0$, twice, same initial layouts and policy sampling seed; the floor $f_t$ is the paired Score difference; this is CL-W43-09's first datum on a shipped validated benchmark. Step 3 (sweep; about 40-60 GPU-h, 5 days): one-at-a-time from $\theta_0$: $h \in \{1, 4, 8.3\}$ ms, position iterations $\in \{4, 16, 32\}$, contact offset at default and 2x, GPU vs CPU PhysX — about 7 settings x 8 tasks x 100 episodes = 5,600 episodes at roughly 25 s each (judgment). Analysis ($0, 1 day): $\delta_{t,k}$ with a paired bootstrap over episodes; a knob 'moves' task $t$ if $|\delta_{t,k}| > \max(f_t, 1.96\,\mathrm{SE})$ and $|\delta_{t,k}| > 0.10$ (the README's claim) or $> 0.04$ (the paper's MAE), both reported; recompute MAE and $r$ against the paper's real column for the tasks among its 22 pairs. Optional step 4 (the engine as a knob, see C-W46-20).
killing_experiment.kills_if: Under every knob within the shipped range, fewer than 2 of the 8 tasks move by more than $\max(f_t, 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}, 0.04)$ and none by more than 0.10: the benchmark's silence about its numerics is harmless at Score granularity and the claim is dead; the residue is the repeat-floor table (CL-W43-09) and a note that the sim-to-sim time-step datum (2610.32277) does not transfer to real-trained policy evaluation. Also dead at step 0 if the runtime exposes no physics setting.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.5: the time step ($h$ from the shipped value to 8.3 ms) moves at least 3 of 8 tasks by more than 0.10, the textile and handover tasks first; the contact offset moves at least 2 (grasp-dependent tasks); position iterations move none above the repeat floor (consistent with 2610.32277 Table 2 and SimuGuard); GPU vs CPU moves none above the floor; the repeat floor itself is 0.02-0.05 at $n = 100$; $r$ recomputed on the 22-pair subset stays above 0.93 under every knob because the shifts are shared within a task class.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: Genie Sim README (fetched 2026-11-15): 'Discrepancy between simulation and real-world test results is less than 10%' with no physics setting named; 2611.15020 sec. II-C: 'Simulation evaluation uses a fixed Genie Sim experimental branch' and nothing on the engine or step; SIMPLER 2405.05941: validity from matching 'the simulator's controller and camera image'; X2Real 2609.27449: 'calibrates simulation visual and physical properties ... 0.84 linear correlation' — the real-to-sim evaluation community treats visuals, controller and assets as the validity axes and numerics as fixed infrastructure; the sim-to-sim community has the opposite datum for RL trackers (2610.32277: 'a wrong timestep').
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If the time step or contact offset moves Scores by more than the claimed discrepancy, a real-to-sim validity number is a property of (policy, scene, engine, setting) and every validation table and leaderboard (RoboColiseum, X2Real, SIMPLER-family) must publish the setting and a sensitivity row — a reporting rule, not a method. If nothing moves above the floor, the sim-to-sim time-step result does not transfer to real-trained policy evaluation at Score granularity, and evaluation-twin builders are entitled to treat numerics as fixed infrastructure, with a citation; either way the lane's 'silent numerics' question gets its first answer on a validated benchmark.

scorecard.target_value: In print: 2611.15020 names 1 ms / TGS 32/1 / solref-solimp and a 25.50 -> 524.61 mm engine swing at the object layer (App. D.3) and reports the task layer from an unnamed setting (sec. II-C); the README's 'less than 10%'; 2609.37771: 'success criteria and simulation settings do not fully capture how acceleration affects task execution'; 2610.32277's 'wrong timestep' datum. Who pays: RoboColiseum and Genie Sim (what to publish with a board), every evaluation-twin builder (X2Real, R2S-Eval, SIMPLER, REALM) choosing what to calibrate, engine builders (NVIDIA Isaac / Newton) whose defaults are being certified by proxy, and reviewers reading a real-to-sim correlation.

Requires a second benchmark (X2Real on Isaac Lab-Arena) at about 60 GPU-h more. Judgment p 0.3.

Requires three benchmarks and an engine owner's endorsement. Judgment p 0.1.

scorecard.relevance: Robotics and learning faculty: direct (what a validated benchmark certifies). Engine builders (NVIDIA Isaac / Newton, Genesis): direct (their defaults are the knobs). Industry (AgiBot, RoboColiseum, evaluation-twin vendors): direct. HAL / evaluators: indirect, as the benchmark-validity shape. Narasimhan route: zero. title: Ninety-eight numbers per arm, which ones moved the task? One-group-at-a-time revert of Genie Sim's robot identification read on the task Score

glossary.identified model: the G2 crsB arm model with 98 unknowns per arm fitted from motor current (70 inertial parameters, 7 armatures, 14 friction coefficients, 7 torque offsets; card eq. 1) plus per-joint PD servo gains $K_{p,j}, K_{d,j}$ (Table C3) and the motion-controller command shaping (5 Hz Butterworth, 11 ms command period).
glossary.URDF model: the CAD-derived model before identification; the paper's 'before' column (Table B2).
glossary.parameter group: one of five sets reverted together: inertial $\boldsymbol{\pi}$, armature $\mathbf{J}_a$, friction $(f_c, f_v)$, servo gains $(K_p, K_d)$, command shaping (filter and period).
glossary.elementary effect: design-of-experiments term (Morris 1991): the change in the response when one factor moves from the baseline with the others held; here the Score change when one group is reverted.
glossary.repeat floor: as in C-W46-18: the Score difference between two identical runs.

statement: Check at step 0 whether the released G2 physics payload carries the identified values printed in Tables 3-4 and C3 (if so the identified model is released; the URDF is the 'before'), then for the released tasks among the paper's 14 G2/Arx pairs evaluate one policy per task (shared with C-W46-18) for $n = 100$ fixed-layout episodes at the identified model and at each one-group-at-a-time revert to the URDF or default value — inertial, armature, friction, servo gains, command shaping — on the benchmark's shipped physics setting. Report per task the elementary effect $\delta_{t,g} = \mathrm{Score}_t(\text{group } g \text{ reverted}) - \mathrm{Score}_t(\text{identified})$ with its paired bootstrap interval against the repeat floor, the concentration $\max_g |\delta_{t,g}| / \sum_g |\delta_{t,g}|$, and the comparison with the paper's own before/after change (MAE 0.0554 to 0.0443 on 14 pairs, 8 shrink / 1 grow / 5 unchanged).
claim: Of the 98 mechanical parameters per arm Genie Sim identified, none moves a task Score above the repeat floor; whatever the identification bought at task level sits in the three controller numbers per joint (servo gains and command shaping), so for a position-controlled arm evaluated by a VLA the calibration worth doing is the controller, not the dynamics.
trick: Put the identified arm back to its CAD values one parameter family at a time and watch the task score: if the score only moves when you touch the servo gains, the 98-parameter identification was decoration.
why_now: 2611.15020 (2026-11-11) printed a full three-stage identification (Tables 3, 4, C1-C3) with a measured task-level before/after that its own text declines to credit ('These robot-level evaluations do not establish an asset-linked benchmark benefit', sec. IV-A; 'Successful execution alone therefore cannot establish an identification benefit', sec. IV-B3); the G2 URDF/USD and per-engine physics payloads are released (README, 2026-11-02); CL-W45-J01 (2026-11-03) asked the per-parameter value question for scene parameters and left the robot class unasked. killing_experiment.design: Step 0 ($0, 1 day): diff the released G2 `robot.usda` / `payloads/Physics/*.usda` against Tables 3-4 and C3 (armature 1.5 / 0.57 / 0.29 kg m^2 groups; $K_p$ 925 ... 200; friction coefficients); if the released payload carries the identified values, the identified model is a released artefact and the URDF is the 'before'; if not, build the identified model from the printed tables where complete (armature, friction, gains, shaping are printed; the 70 inertial parameters are in Tables C1-C2 'complete joint/family breakdown' — check completeness) and cost the inertial group as unbuildable if the table is partial. Arithmetic now ($0): the paper's MAE drop of 0.011 over 14 pairs lies below the per-pair binomial-bound SE (0.05-0.09) and near the SE of the 14-pair mean (about 0.017); the sign test 8 shrink / 1 grow (ties dropped) gives $p \approx 0.04$ — marginal, so the direction is weakly in print and the attribution is not. Step 1 (policies; shared with C-W46-18, 0-60 GPU-h): the released tasks among the 14 G2/Arx pairs, pi0.5 SFT on real AgiBot World episodes where they exist. Step 2 (about 30-40 GPU-h, 4 days): 6 arms (identified + 5 reverts) x up to 8 tasks x 100 episodes with fixed layouts; the repeat floor from C-W46-18 step 2 or run here (6 GPU-h). Analysis ($0, 1 day): $\delta_{t,g}$, paired bootstrap, concentration, and a Morris-style ranking of groups by $|\delta|$ across tasks.
killing_experiment.kills_if: Every group, including servo gains and command shaping, moves every task Score by less than $\max(f_t, 1.96\,\mathrm{SE})$: the identification's task-level effect is inside the engine's own noise for all 98 + controller numbers, the paper's hedge is confirmed numerically and there is nothing to concentrate — dead as a value-concentration probe (the residue is a footnote: the published before/after improvement is a re-run noise number). Also dead if the mechanical groups move Scores by more than the controller group on most tasks (the pre-registered direction is reversed; CL-W45-J01's robot-class extension is then false, which is informative for the claim). Dead at step 0 if neither the payload nor the printed tables give a buildable identified model.

title: The engine swing at the task layer: the same Genie Sim task and policy on the PhysX and Newton runtimes the platform ships, read against the real-sim gap

glossary.model-form disagreement: the lane's third V&V leg — the difference between two engines' outputs on the same scene at identical physical parameters; the paper measured it at the object layer (sponge 25.50 mm in MuJoCo, 524.61 mm in PhysX, App. D.3) and never at the task layer.
glossary.task-selected runtime: Genie Sim's per-task choice of engine: 'direct Isaac evaluation, managed Newton wok evaluation, and native MuJoCo Rubik execution' (README).
glossary.per-engine physics payload: the AS3 asset layout's `payloads/Physics/{physics,physx,mujoco}.usda`: one robot description with engine-specific physics files (README).

statement: At step 0 list the released benchmark tasks that already carry two runtime payloads (PhysX and Newton, or PhysX and MuJoCo) and choose up to 6 contact-rich ones; where a chosen task has one runtime, port it to the second at identical physical parameters only if the port is a configuration change (no new assets), else drop it. Evaluate one policy per task (shared with C-W46-18) for $n = 100$ fixed-layout episodes on each runtime at that runtime's shipped setting and report the cross-engine Score disagreement $\epsilon_t = \mathrm{Score}_t(\mathrm{engine\ B}) - \mathrm{Score}_t(\mathrm{engine\ A})$ with its paired bootstrap interval against the repeat floor of each engine and against the paper's real-sim gap for that task where it is one of the 22 pairs.
claim: On Genie Sim Benchmark, swapping the shipped engine at identical physical parameters moves the simulated Score of contact-rich tasks by more than the published real-sim gap for those tasks, so which engine scored a task is part of the validity number and the benchmark does not say which it was.
trick: The paper showed one sponge going from 2.5 cm wrong to 52 cm wrong when the engine changed and the parameters did not; run the whole task on both engines the platform ships and see whether the task score moves more than the real-sim gap the paper reports.
why_now: Genie Sim v3.5.0 (2026-11-02, README fetched) ships task-selected runtimes and per-engine physics payloads, so an engine swap on a validated benchmark task is a configuration change for the first time; 2611.15020 (2026-11-11) measured the object-layer swing and named the task-layer engine nowhere; Alloy 2611.16312 (2026-11-12) and HolidayFactory 2611.11789 (2026-11-09) are two more Newton-based engines arriving under robot benchmarks this week, so the engine behind a Score is becoming a free variable.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 ($0, 2 days): from the released task list and `payloads/Physics/`, count tasks with two runtimes; read each runtime's shipped setting; write the pre-registered task set (up to 6, contact-rich first; the wok task if it is the Newton one). Dead at step 0 if fewer than 3 released tasks run on two runtimes without new assets. Step 1 (policies; shared with C-W46-18). Step 2 (about 12-18 GPU-h, 3 days): 2 engines x 6 tasks x 100 episodes plus a repeat run per engine (another 12 GPU-h if not already in C-W46-18). Analysis ($0, 1 day): $\epsilon_t$ with paired bootstrap; a task 'disagrees' if $|\epsilon_t| > \max(f_t^A, f_t^B, 1.96\,\mathrm{SE})$; compare with the paper's $|\Delta_t|$ (0.00-0.11) and MAE 0.04.
killing_experiment.kills_if: On every two-runtime task $|\epsilon_t|$ is below $\max(f_t^A, f_t^B, 1.96\,\mathrm{SE})$ or below the paper's real-sim gap for that task: model-form error is inside the validation's own gap at Score granularity and the engine's name is a footnote. Also dead at step 0 if fewer than 3 released tasks run on two runtimes without porting assets (then the probe is a build, not a measurement, and is parked with that trigger).

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.45: on textile or deformable tasks (where the Newton path exists because PhysX lacks cloth) the swap is not even possible at identical parameters, so the measurable set is rigid contact-rich tasks (stacking, handover, drawer); there $|\epsilon_t| > 0.10$ on at least 2 of the measurable tasks, driven by contact-offset and friction-model differences, with pick-and-place tasks inside the floor.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: 2611.15020 App. D.3: 'The source path does not express MuJoCo solref/solimp equivalently ... Geometry, initialization, robot/observation calibration and numerical differences remain potential contributors' — the authors treat the object-layer swing as a mapping problem, not as a property of the task Scores; the README quotes one '<10%' discrepancy for the whole benchmark across three runtimes; PolySim 2510.01708 and ROBOGATE (CL-W43-J04 kill record) measured cross-engine gaps for sim-trained RL policies, where exploitation of the training engine is the mechanism; for real-trained policies evaluated across platforms, 2606.10366 compared different platforms with different assets, not one scene with the engine swapped.

If the swing is inside the floor on every measurable task, rigid-contact model-form error is a non-issue for VLA evaluation at Score granularity and the object-layer swing does not propagate — a datum the engine builders cite.
